power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: We assessed potential associations between migraine and complete blood cell count (CBC) data in three large population-based studies.
Platelets are thought to be involved in migraine pathology through increased activation during an attack.
Migraine attacks are often treated with NSAIDs that inhibit platelets, or triptans that target serotonin receptors, with serotonin being most highly expressed in circulation within platelet granules.
However, the exact role of platelets in migraine remains unclear.
The UK BioBank (UKBB) has CBC data available from baseline blood samples and migraine diagnoses were obtained through self-report and electronic health records.

text.text: However, a major limitation to most prior work is relatively modest sample sizes and a lack of replication samples.
Thus, most were underpowered to detect small or moderate associations between cell counts, cell count ratios, and migraine.
Based on the previous literature, we hypothesized that platelet cell counts and cell ratios indicative of altered immune function are associated with migraine.
We explored these hypotheses in larger cohorts and biobanks than prior studies, including a replication design.
The UK Biobank collected health data from over 500,000 people, including blood samples and lifestyle information [15] .

text.text: Cell counts were measured at baseline.
Migraine outcome was defined by self-report and ICD9 (3460, 3461, 3462, 3468, 3469) and ICD10 (G43.0, G43.1, for use under a CC0 license.
G43.2, G43.3, G43.8, G43.9) codes at baseline and during follow-up.
Incident cases had the same ICD codes with an occurrence later than the baseline date, or if the self-reported age at occurrence was older than baseline age.

We assessed mean platelet volume (MPV), platelet count (PLT), lymphocyte (LYM), monocyte (MON), neutrophil (NEU), hemoglobin (HGB), red blood cell distribution width (RDW), white blood cell count (WBC) and nine cell count ratios constructed among these eight cell count traits.
The cell count ratios (MPV.PLT, PLT.LYM, PLT.MON, PLT.NEU, HGB.RDW, RDW.PLT, NEU.LYM, MON.LYM, WBC.MPV) were selected based on biomarker studies.
In ratio names (e.g.
MPV.PLT), the first cell count (MPV) was the numerator, and the second cell count (PLT) was the denominator.
Log transformation was applied to the derived cell count ratios [16] .

text.text: Samples with NEU=0, LYM=0, without genetic data for inferring ancestry, or withdrawn from participation were excluded.
Association analysis for the cell counts/ratios was restricted to samples with complete data on all 8 primary cell count measures.
Based on the available data, 467,258 people were included in the analysis, with 18,919 migraine cases (including 4,580 incident cases) and 448,339 controls.

Migraine is known to have sex differences in prevalence, with women making up most migraine cases.
This difference is first seen during puberty, when the prevalence of migraine increases in both sexes, but more so in women [22 23].

text.text: Many women experience menstrual related migraine, and migraine frequency and severity may improve with pregnancy and menopause [23] .

text.text: Interestingly, platelet count appears relatively similar in males and females until around the age of fourteen, and then females start to have higher platelet counts, suggesting that puberty might affect platelet production [24] .

text.text: The onset of puberty in females is marked by an increase in estrogen.
Estrogen is also thought to influence platelet count [25 26] , specifically by increasing it, as estrogen signaling is known to promote hematopoiesis and erythropoiesis [27] .

text.text: It is possible that the increase in platelet count that occurs in females during puberty could be connected to the increased prevalence of migraine that occurs at about the same time.

In our study however, we observed higher platelet counts were associated with increased migraine prevalence in both women and men, suggesting that sex-differences in migraine and platelet counts alone do not fully account for the association between them.
Other migraine studies have also observed associations between higher platelet count and migraine.
Platelet count and migraine with aura were positively, but weakly, associated in the population-based Rotterdam study [10] .

Despite this, the findings point to a general idea of higher platelet count playing a role in headaches and headache development, which would encompass migraine.
Essential thrombocythemia (ET) is a medical condition characterized by an overproduction of platelets and an extremely high platelet count.
Interestingly, one of the common manifestations of this disorder is headaches, more specifically migraine with aura-like headaches [11 31] .

text.text: Antiaggregating and antiplatelet medications have been shown to reduce the frequency and severity of the migraine-like headaches or even stop them in people with ET [11 32].

text.text: Low-dose aspirin has also been shown to have a very modest effect on reducing migraine frequency and other related characteristics [33] , lending more support to the idea that antiplatelet medications can be used for migraine.

text.text: These observations seem to point to platelets and high platelet count being involved in migraine pathology, which is in line with the associations seen in our data.
Although ET is a very extreme case of high platelet count, the associations seen lend their support to increased platelet count playing a role in the development and onset of migraine.
A few studies did not observe an association between platelet count and migraine [34 35] .

text.text: However, differences in sample sizes, which tend to be small, participant selection (headache clinic vs emergency department vs population-based study), whether or not a healthy control population is included, types of headache included (migraine in general, migraine with and without aura, tension-type), and whether or not the participant is experiencing a migraine attack for use under a CC0 license.
during the blood draw may explain some of the difference seen across studies.
In contrast, our study was much larger and more well-powered to detect more modest associations.
This study has several limitations.
A majority of the migraine data was self-reported, and we lack information on duration, frequency, or subtype of migraine.
This extends into the incident cases, as we are unable to determine whether or not these cases are truly new reports from people who have never previously reported migraine.
Several studies have shown differences in platelet activity based on subtype, but this could not be included in this analysis.
Our sample was primarily composed of individuals of European ancestry so the generalizability to other groups may be limited.
However, among the population studies to date of platelet count/MPV this study also ranks as one of the largest to our knowledge.
Our results support the hypothesis that platelets may have a contributory role in the development of migraine among both men and women.

However, elucidation of more precise roles of platelets in migraine and their utility as one component of prediction of migraine attacks will require large, prospective studies with both repeated platelet measurements and more detailed recording of migraine and headache recurrence and symptomatic subtyping.
